# Block 1: Project-based workflows {.unnumbered} The single most common reason a shared script fails on someone else's computer is a file path. A line like `read.csv("C:/Users/me/thesis/data/penguins.csv")` is a statement about *your* machine, not about the analysis. The fix is to make the project, not your home directory, the centre of the universe. ## Why a project An RStudio project is a folder with an `.Rproj` marker file; in Positron, a project is simply a folder you open (**File → Open Folder**), no `.Rproj` file needed. Opening it does two useful things automatically: it sets the working directory to the project folder, and it points the file browser there. Every path you write can then be relative to the project root, which means the project can be zipped, shared, or moved to another operating system and still run without editing a single path. To create one: **File → New Project → New Directory → New Project**, name it, and click **Create Project**. RStudio leaves an `.Rproj` file in the folder. Double-clicking that file opens a fresh session pointed at the project. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![A typical R project layout](images/project.png){fig-align='center' width=80%} ::: ::: ## Absolute versus relative paths An **absolute path** spells out the full location from the root of the disk: ``` /home/your-username/project/data/raw/penguins.csv ``` It breaks the moment anyone else opens your code, because nobody else has your directory structure. A **relative path** is relative to the project root, so it travels with the project: ``` data/raw/penguins.csv ``` ## A sensible layout Organise each project into its own folder with a predictable structure. The convention we follow all day (we will come back to this on Day 2!): ``` my-project.Rproj |- data/ | |- raw/ # read-only; never edited by code | |- processed/ # outputs of cleaning |- R/ | |- functions/ # function definitions only | |- scripts/ # numbered analysis scripts |- outputs/ | |- figures/ | |- tables/ ``` The principle that does the most work here is *raw data is read-only*. Cleaning scripts read from `data/raw/` and write to `data/processed/`; they never overwrite the original. If a clean goes wrong, the source of truth is untouched. ## Setting up a new project Start a new R project whenever you begin a distinct task, research project or analysis. This keeps your work organised, which helps most when you need to collaborate, share the work or come back to it later. :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Your turn :::: ::::{.task-container} Set up your first R project: * [ ] 1. Go to "File" in the RStudio menu. * [ ] 2. Select "New Project..." * [ ] 3. Choose a project type or create a new directory for the project. * [ ] 4. Give it a name "Penguins" * [ ] 5. Click "Create Project." The new project will be created with a .Rproj file. You can open it by double-clicking on this file or by using the "File" menu in RStudio. :::: ::: :::{.callout-warning} NEVER move the .Rproj file; this may stop your workspace from opening properly. ::: More on projects can be found in the [R4DS](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/workflow-scripts.html#projects) book. ## Build a project structure Let's create the folder structure above. There are several ways to do this: :::{.panel-tabset} ## IDE * Create the following folders using the + New Folder button in the Files tab * data/raw * data/processed * R/functions * R/scripts * outputs ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Making folders](images/new-folders.png){fig-align='center' width=80%} ::: ::: :::{.callout-warning} R is case-sensitive and whitespace-sensitive, so type everything EXACTLY as printed here ::: ## Base R ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # dir.create makes directories # unless specified it is not "recursive" dir.create("data/raw", recursive = TRUE) dir.create("data/processed", recursive = TRUE) dir.create("R/functions", recursive = TRUE) dir.create("R/scripts", recursive = TRUE) dir.create("outputs") ``` ::: ## `fs` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # Load the package library(fs) # Create standard folders dir_create("data", c("raw", "processed")) # creates dir recursively as standard dir_create("R", c("functions", "scripts")) # for your R code dir_create("outputs") # for figures and tables ``` ::: Run `fs::dir_tree()` to print a nicely formatted directory tree. It is a quick sanity check before and after you move files around. The `fs` @R-fs package behaves the same on every operating system, and it works safely: it will not overwrite files or folders unless you explicitly ask it to. ::: Separate subfolders keep the project tidy, make files harder to lose, and make it easy to tell R exactly where to find your data. You might also want to keep any wider reading or other information you have gathered that is relevant to the project. :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Your turn :::: ::::{.task-container} Try creating subdirectories for the outputs folder :::: :::
::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} subdir <- c("figures", "tables") fs::dir_create("outputs", subdir) ``` :::
## The `here` package Even inside a project, paths written with `\\` only work on Windows, and relative paths break if you run code from a subdirectory. `here::here()` builds a path from the project root regardless of where the code is called from or which operating system runs it. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # Fragile: relative to wherever the session happens to sit raw_data <- readr::read_csv("data/raw/penguins.csv") # Robust: built from the project root every time library(here) raw_data <- readr::read_csv(here("data", "raw", "penguins.csv")) ``` ::: `here()` finds the root by looking for the `.Rproj` file (or a `.here` file), so it does not depend on the working directory. We recommend using an RStudio project *and* `here()` together. Either alone helps; both together is robust. :::{.callout-note} Further reading on `here`: the package's own rationale at sets out the argument better than we can here. The short version: a path is part of your code, and code should not assume it knows where it lives. ::: ### Activity: de-path a script :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} De-path a script :::: ::::{.task-container} Below is the opening of a script written without a project. Rewrite it so it would run unchanged on a colleague's machine. You should change two things: the working directory line, and the path. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} setwd("/Users/sam/Documents/penguin_thesis/") penguins_raw <- read.csv("/Users/sam/Documents/penguin_thesis/data/raw/penguins.csv") ``` ::: :::: :::
::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # No setwd() at all: open the project instead, which sets the directory for you. library(here) library(tidyverse) penguins_raw <- readr::read_csv(here("data", "raw", "penguins.csv")) ``` ::: The `setwd()` line is deleted entirely, not replaced. Setting the working directory is the project's job, not the script's. The path is rebuilt from the project root with `here()`, so it no longer mentions any user or machine. `read_csv()` comes from the `readr` package, which is part of the tidyverse, so loading `tidyverse` covers it. You could load `readr` on its own instead; we load `tidyverse` because it is a common choice for data analysis.
## Blank slates A clean analysis should not depend on hidden state left over from a previous session: a package you attached by hand, an object you created interactively, an option you set and forgot. Many scripts open with `rm(list = ls())` in an attempt to start clean, but this is a weak guarantee. It removes user-created objects but does **not** detach packages, reset options, or change the working directory. The session is still contaminated. The reliable habit is to **restart R** (Session → Restart R, or `Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+F10`) and rerun the script from the top. If the analysis runs correctly from a fresh session, it is reproducible; if it needs objects that exist only because of something you did by hand earlier, you find out immediately rather than six months later. Treat the script, not the workspace, as the record of what you did. :::{.callout-tip} Turn off workspace saving so a stale `.RData` never loads silently. In Tools → Global Options → General, set "Save workspace to .RData on exit" to **Never**, and untick "Restore .RData into workspace at startup". Now every session starts blank, and the only way to recreate your objects is to run your code. ::: ## `renv`: pinning package versions A project that runs today can break next year if a package changes its behaviour. `renv` records the exact package versions a project uses, in a project-local library, so the environment can be reconstructed later or on another machine. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # Once per project: create a project-local library and record current versions renv::init() # Install into the project library (not the global one) renv::install("dplyr") # After installing or updating anything, record the new state renv::snapshot() # On another machine, or after things break, rebuild the recorded environment renv::restore() ``` ::: `renv::status()` reports whether the lockfile and the library agree. By default `renv::snapshot()` records only the packages your project's code actually uses: it scans your scripts and Quarto files for `library()`, `require()` and `pkg::fn()` calls. Installing a package is not enough; if no file in the project uses it, it will not appear in `renv.lock`. This means the lockfile captures what you use rather than everything installed. :::{.callout-note} `renv` is a large step towards reproducibility, not a complete guarantee. It notes the R version you used in `renv.lock`, but it does not reinstall that version for you. For stronger guarantees, tools such as `rig` (switching R versions) or Docker (capturing the whole environment) exist, but they are beyond today's scope. For most analysis projects, a project plus `here()` plus `renv` is enough. ::: ### Activity: initialise a project environment :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Initialise a project environment :::: ::::{.task-container} In a fresh project, run `renv::init()`, then `renv::install("janitor")`. Before you snapshot, create a script (for example `R/scripts/01_clean.R`) containing `library(janitor)` and save it: renv only records packages your code uses. Now run `renv::snapshot()`. Open `renv.lock` in a text editor and find the entry for `janitor`. What information is recorded about it, and why would a collaborator need that exact information to reproduce your analysis? What happens if you run `renv::snapshot()` *without* the script? :::: ::: :::{.callout-note} **Where this leaves us.** We now have a project that runs anywhere, reads its data by relative path, starts from a blank slate, and pins its package versions. Everything from here assumes you are working inside such a project. The rest of the day fills it with well-organised analytical code. :::
